title: Peter Chan’s Toronto-Bound ‘The Road Not Taken’ Boards Moebius Entertainment for International Sales
description: Hong Kong-based Moebius Entertainment has boarded Peter Ho-Sun Chan’s new film, “The Road Not Taken,” picking up international sales rights ahead of
body:
Hong Kong-based Moebius Entertainment has boarded Peter Ho-Sun Chan’s new film, “The Road Not Taken,” picking up international sales rights ahead of its bow in the Special Presentations lineup at the Toronto Film Festival.

	Chan directs Zhou Xun, Wen Qi, Tian Zhuangzhuang and Wang Xiao in the drama, which centers on early-onset Alzheimer disease. Zhou plays Jia Jia, a television host whose outwardly composed career masks a marriage to a wildlife conservationist that is coming apart. Fumbling the term “artificial intelligence” for “artificial talent” during a live panel, she initially puts the slip down to exhaustion, but the moment marks the start of symptoms that grow harder to ignore. As her condition advances, the story folds in her strained bonds with her daughter, played by Wen Qi, and her father, played by Fifth Generation filmmaker Tian Zhuangzhuang. 
	

	The Toronto berth marks a return to the festival for Chan, whose “She Has No Name” screened last year. Fred Tsui, founder and chief executive of Moebius Entertainment, first worked with Chan as executive producer on that film and its international rollout, a partnership that carries over to “The Road Not Taken.”


	Moebius closed the deal for “The Road Not Taken” before Tsui’s appointment as executive director of the Hong Kong International Film Festival Society. Tsui is stepping back from new sales projects as he moves into that role, though “The Road Not Taken” was already committed to Moebius beforehand, and the company will steer its international sales campaign and coordinate with the filmmakers on rolling the film out globally. Tsui is set to begin as HKIFFS executive director on Sept. 23, taking over from Albert Lee.
	

	“Peter Chan is a filmmaker of extraordinary emotional precision and global reach,” said Tsui. “Following our work together on ‘She Has No Name,’ it is a pleasure to continue that relationship with ‘The Road Not Taken.’ Its world premiere at TIFF offers an exceptional platform for the film’s first encounter with international audiences.”

	Moebius will unveil “The Road Not Taken” for buyers and programmers during the Toronto market, taking on sales duties in every territory beyond the film’s home turf.

	Moebius Entertainment, based in Hong Kong, represents distinctive Asian and international titles, working with filmmakers and producers to craft tailored festival, sales and distribution plans in markets worldwide.

schema.headline: Peter Chan’s Toronto-Bound ‘The Road Not Taken’ Boards Moebius Entertainment for International Sales

title: ‘The Best Mother in the World’ Standout Shirley Cruz to Star in Clara Ferrer and Tainá Bevilacqua’s Trans Coming-of-Age ‘The She-Devil’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Shirley Cruz, who delivered an acclaimed central performance in Anna Muylaert’s 2025 Berlinale drama “The Best Mother in the World,” is set to star
body:
Shirley Cruz, who delivered an acclaimed central performance in Anna Muylaert’s 2025 Berlinale drama “The Best Mother in the World,” is set to star in Clara Ferrer and Tainá Bevilacqua’s “The She-Devil.” 

	“The She-Devil” is currently in development, with a short film taking place in the same universe, titled “The Death of the She-Devil,” currently in post-production. Both films star Cruz as Auntl lara, with Ferrer writing. Amina Sophia Nogueira will executive produce for Capivara Movies, with Laura Fazoli as producer and Retrato Filmes already on board as a Brazilian distributor. The short film was made in partnership with Cajamanga and Dobra. 
	

	The coming-of-age feature is an adaptation of the eponymous book by Eli Lemos de Oliveira, a poetic work of autofiction centered on a young trans man raised in a working-class community of Rio de Janeiro, who explores masculinity through the female figures in his life. The film will be set in the ’90s, and will trail the 11-year-old Araí as he develops an obsession with an imaginary killer who attacks girls in their neighborhood. At first determined to capture him, little by little Araí starts to understand, and eventually, to identify with the villain.


	Speaking with Variety out of Locarno, where she took part in the festival’s prestigious networking program Match Me!, Nogueira saId the story is set “in a specific place, but deals with universal themes we believe resonate globally.” “Everyone had, or wishes they’d had, an Aunt lara when they were young, and hopes to be that person for the children in their lives.”
	

	“This is the story of a child who struggles against the femininity assigned to them at birth while learning misogyny, but who can only reconcile with masculinity through the love for the most important woman in their life: lara, an aunt who offers guidance and inspiration through her transgressive way of living,” added Ferrer.

	Bevilacqua said she wanted to adapt the book from the very first time she read it, with the author happily agreeing to it. “Our vision for the film, which we’ve playfully christened ‘contemporary working-class baroque,’ is a plunge into the subjectivity of a protagonist in crisis, who sees the world in opposing extremes — the familiar and the unknown, the sacred and the profane, enchantment and horror — which are integrated in the character of Iara,” she notes.

	Nogueira said having Cruz on their first set under Capivara Films “is an enormous privilege.” “I couldn’t have asked for a better way to start.”

	“Shirley Cruz is an actress of extraordinary sensitivity, bringing complexity, tenderness and strength to Tia Iara, a woman who must help her young niece navigate the difficult passage from childhood into adulthood,” Ferrer and Bevilacqua added. 

	Clara Ferrer has directed several short films and her first feature as a screenwriter, “Four Girls,” premiered earlier this year at the Berlinale. Tainá Bevilacqua first began working with Ferrer in 2018 as the star of Ferrer’s debut short film, “A Casa de Ana.” Since then, she has continued to work on award-winning short films. 

	Capivara Movies is an independent production company based in Rio de Janeiro, founded in 2024 by Laura Fazoli. It develops Brazilian films and series with international potential, working with established filmmakers, including Sandra Kogut and Gabriela Amaral Almeida, as well as emerging voices such as Ferrer and Bevilacqua.

	Nogueira told Variety how Capivara works across “two complementary lines.” “One focuses on larger-scale projects, combining private investment, international co-production, and partnerships with broadcasters and streaming platforms. The other is dedicated to auteur cinema, built on public funding complemented by international resources.”

	“Across both, we believe international co-production is key to the kind of cinema we want to make, and we build every project for international circulation from the earliest stage, working closely with our filmmakers,” she added. “Our goal is a catalog that combines artistic ambition with audience reach, spread across platforms and territories.”

schema.headline: ‘The Best Mother in the World’ Standout Shirley Cruz to Star in Clara Ferrer and Tainá Bevilacqua’s Trans Coming-of-Age ‘The She-Devil’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Jeremy Strong Wrote to Mark Zuckerberg After Being Cast in ‘Social Reckoning’ Even Though ‘He’s a Reviled Person’; Actor Spent 7 Months Talking in Polish Accent for Next Role
description: Jeremy Strong graces the latest cover of GQ magazine (and the first issue published under new global editorial director Adam Baidawi), in which he s
body:
Jeremy Strong graces the latest cover of GQ magazine (and the first issue published under new global editorial director Adam Baidawi), in which he speaks out for the first time on taking over the role of Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Jesse Eisenberg played the controversial tech titan in “The Social Network” and scored an Oscar nomination. Strong stars as Zuckerberg in writer-director Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up piece “The Social Reckoning.” 
	

	Sorkin originally asked Eisenberg if he wanted to reprise Zuckerberg in the new movie, to which the actor declined because he no longer “wants to be associated” with the Facebook co-founder. At the same time, Strong ran into Sorkin at an Oscars season party and told him to call him should Eisenberg not return.


	“It’s the kind of role that fascinates me,” Strong told GQ about throwing his hat into the ring to play Zuckerberg. “It’s like Sebastian [Stan] playing Trump. You are wearing the cape. It’s like Jeremy [Allen White] playing Bruce [Springsteen]. It’s like, the perils of that could not be greater. To commit to it, and to be free within it, is a great challenge… Listen, I know that he is a reviled person and not a popular person in our culture, but I do not think you should have an actor playing him who wants to set out to condemn him.”

	Strong confirmed that he reached out to Zuckerberg after accepting the role in “The Social Reckoning.” The Facebook CEO wrote back, but Strong would not reveal what he said.

	“I wrote to him — I’m probably going to give Sony an aneurysm — I sent him an email,” Strong said. “Just to say that I take this responsibility very seriously, and the veracity of it seriously, and I’m approaching it with respect.” 
	

	Per GQ: “Strong wanted to absorb everything he could — podcasts, magazine interviews, tech-summit talks, and ideas-festival conversations. He watched footage of Zuckerberg testifying before Congress ‘until my eyes fell out of my head,’ trying to internalize it. He doesn’t do social media, but he signed up for a Facebook account to read through Zuckerberg’s posts from the beginning, a longitudinal record of Zuckerberg’s evolution, in the gap between the two films, into a ‘wartime CEO.'”

	The first trailer for “The Social Reckoning” was released by Sony in June to a polarizing degree of responses. When it was brought to Strong’s attention that some social media users predicted an Oscar nom in his future for playing Zuckerberg while others predicted a Razzie nom, the actor responded: “I thought that was the greatest endorsement. Because to me, it was like — listen, I’ll be sad if I win a Razzie, but that’s the place you want to be. That’s the wager you have to make. To me, that means, Okay, I put it on the line enough.”

	As is the case with every Strong project, the actor went full Method to play Zuckerberg and spoke only as the Facebook CEO for the entirety of production. As the actor’s friend Bradley Cooper told GQ: “I’ve talked to Mark Zuckerberg many times — I had a whole friendship with Mark Zuckerberg, and Mark Zuckerberg has no idea.”

	In fact, Strong was in Method actor mode during his GQ interview and spoke only in a Polish accent amid the continued production of “The Boys from Brazil.” Strong is headlining the latest film adaptation of Ira Levin’s 1976 novel as a globe-trotting Nazi hunter. The Emmy winner spent seven months speaking in a Polish accent during filming, whether he was on set or just on the phone with friends like Cooper or collaborators like Aaron Sorkin.

	“He called me six or eight weeks ago, and without any introduction, he was just speaking as an Eastern European Nazi hunter, talking to me about the movie we had just made, without saying, ‘Hey, listen, this is going to sound strange, but.…’” Sorkin noted.

	“The Social Reckoning” opens in theaters Oct. 9. Head over to GQ’s website to read Strong’s cover in its entirety.

schema.headline: Jeremy Strong Wrote to Mark Zuckerberg After Being Cast in ‘Social Reckoning’ Even Though ‘He’s a Reviled Person’; Actor Spent 7 Months Talking in Polish Accent for Next Role

title: ‘Wandering Trees’ Review: Iconoclastic Director Salvatore Mereu Tries a Newly Minted Fairyale, but Only Fitfully Finds Magic
description: In fairy tales, we never question why the beautiful princess is marrying a horrible prince: Part of the pact readers make with such stories is that
body:
In fairy tales, we never question why the beautiful princess is marrying a horrible prince: Part of the pact readers make with such stories is that we accept these situations at face value. In real life though, when presented with a woman joining herself to a nasty piece of work, we need to know why. Comedies aside, combining these two literary forms creates minefields for a writer because the moment disbelief spreads like mold, the most fantastically built Cinderella castle collapses. “Wandering Trees,” Salvatore Mereu‘s new three-hour film, is unmistakably part of the iconoclastic director’s world, with its almost metaphysical approach to Sardinians’ relationship to the land, but a major tonal clash between the pronounced fairy-tale structure and the realistic elements trips up his customary mastery in handling complex narratives.
	

	Long an outlier in the Italian cinema landscape, Mereu’s films (“Assandira,” “Pretty Butterflies,” etc.) are intimately bound up in the distinct natural rhythms of his island home. Harnessing a signature cinematic eye to a near-mystical reverence for the land and its ancient traditions, he’s a filmmaker whose work stands in resistance to Italianization, like a bold sociologist fighting for a rural way of life fast becoming extinct. While he’s never shied away from narrative experimentation, he’s also never been so hampered by a fundamental misunderstanding of the dramatic contract. His sense of beauty is unsullied, his respect for nature in all its forms unshaken, but when the question “why” insistently encroaches on audience involvement, there’s a problem.
	

	“To be friends with the animals is to be a friend and a child of the world, connected to it, nourished by it, belonging to it.” The line is Ursula K. Le Guin’s, but it could also be spoken by Piero Arca (Alessandro Haber), a man of the land — the word “peasant” in English has unfortunate connotations that don’t correspond to the Italian “contadino” — whose life is devoted to nurturing rescued animals together with his young son Giuliano (Lupo Barbiero). The boy lives in two worlds: the one at home, where donkey brays, pig squeals and a tortoise interrupt his homework, and school, like any other kid.

	But for some people in the neighborhood, Giuliano and Piero aren’t like the others. Their symbiotic devotion to the land and respect for all creatures make them pariahs, targets not just of verbal attacks but threatening gunshots. Particular animosity comes from Sebastiano Nonne (Massimo Popolizio), of a military family whose large house has a monarcho-fascist sancta sanctorum and is full of taxidermied animals. His sensitive book-hound son Emiliano (Lorenzo Urso) is Giuliano’s best friend, but Sebastiano forbids him from associating with the Arca family.

	By now Mereu’s demarcations are fairly apparent: people at one with nature versus those who kill, and sensitivity versus cruelty. (Audiences could logically expect another contrast between the working and upper classes, but as we’ll see, fairy tales need their princesses.) When Piero brings Giuliano to a forest called “The Children” (“I Bambini”), we’re bracing ourselves for a magical realism moment.

	But no, not quite yet. Time jumps ahead and we meet Edoardo Branca (Alberto Cracco), a bookish old man who wears nice cardigans and smiles a lot in his aristocratic palazzo. His daughter Maddalena (Giulia Maenza) is our princess; she may not have a title, but she has the house and more importantly, she has a beauty and grace that could have come straight out of a storybook. Her boyfriend is nasty Sebastiano’s older soldier son Michelangelo (Lorenzo Richelmy), a true chip off the old block. She’s spontaneous and playful, he’s rigid and rulebound. For Emiliano, tormentedly poetic, it’s not easy having such a brother. Or father, for that matter, especially after Sebastiano repeatedly slams his son’s head against a sink.
	

	Then one day, Giuliano (now played by an excellent Romeo Perrone) comes home to discover all the animals massacred and his father gone. Setting out to search for him, Giuliano heads to “The Children,” only this time the children appear, ragtag forest dwellers who first tell him to leave but then, like a multitude of junior Calypsos, don’t want him to go. While all this is happening, Mereu’s also keeping track of Maddalena and Michelangelo, until the inevitable moment when the princess meets the woodsman and the spell can be broken.

	While it’s a given that fairy tales have a built-in element of predictability, “Wandering Trees” wants to have it both ways: far too many elements are screamingly obvious, like the stuffed buzzards in the Nonne house, and of course young Giuliano studies Giacomo Leopardi’s poem “The Infinite” (“L’Infinito”), the most recognizable paean to nature in all of Italian literature. Poor Emiliano’s character cries out for development, while Maddalena’s two sisters seem tossed in simply because storybook princesses always have sisters, don’t they?

	Perhaps the fault lies in Alberto Capitta’s novel (he also co-wrote the script), but the point of adaptations is to make them work on screen. Mereu’s sure hand with his actors is a saving grace, with Perrone and Maenza particularly well-cast, and DP Francesco Piras lights them to perfection while being in perfect synch with the director’s reverence for the natural world. The problem isn’t the wandering trees, but the wandering narrative, which needs deeper roots.

schema.headline: ‘Wandering Trees’ Review: Iconoclastic Director Salvatore Mereu Tries a Newly Minted Fairyale, but Only Fitfully Finds Magic

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2 Sets September Date
description: “Saturday Night Live U.K.” will launch its second season on Sky and Now starting Sept. 12, the broadcaster announced, kicking off a run of six new e
body:
“Saturday Night Live U.K.” will launch its second season on Sky and Now starting Sept. 12, the broadcaster announced, kicking off a run of six new episodes following the show’s debut season earlier this year.

	A trailer for the new season has been released, and additional episodes are planned for early 2027 beyond the initial six-episode run. As in the debut season, every episode will pair a new celebrity host with a musical guest, alongside topical sketches, live musical performances and a British spin on “Weekend Update.”
	

	Audience tickets will open through a ballot on Aug. 14.


	The six confirmed episodes are set to air on Sept. 12, Sept. 19, Sept. 26, Oct. 10, Oct. 17 and Oct. 24.

	All 11 cast members from the inaugural season are returning: Hammed Animashaun, Ayoade Bamgboye, Larry Dean, Celeste Dring, George Fouracres, Ania Magliano, Annabel Marlow, Al Nash, Jack Shep, Emma Sidi and Paddy Young.

	There are several changes behind the scenes for the new season. Laura Claxton steps up to co-head writer alongside Jonno Johnson, who remains head writer. Director Liz Clare is back for a second season, costume designer Heather MacVean joins the team for the first time, and Sinead Oldnall takes charge of onscreen talent for the U.K. production.

	Universal Television Alternative Studio’s U.K. arm and Broadway Video produce the series for Sky and NOW, with Lorne Michaels executive producing and James Longman leading production. Helen Kruger Bratt heads UTAS U.K. Productions as managing director, with Andy Charles Smith producing for the label, Shanna Baynard overseeing production and Hannah Peddar serving as production executive.
	

	Phil Edgar-Jones, Sky’s executive director of unscripted originals, commissioned the series, with Alex Moody, the broadcaster’s head of comedy commissioning, handling the second-season order for Sky Studios CEO and chief content officer Cecile Frot-Coutaz.

title: U.K.’s Largest Harry Potter Store Opening in London Ahead of HBO Series Launch
description: With Harry Potter excitement expected to reach fever pitch once more later this year with the launch of HBO’s new TV series, Warner Bros. is going b
body:
With Harry Potter excitement expected to reach fever pitch once more later this year with the launch of HBO’s new TV series, Warner Bros. is going big on the merch — and just in time for Christmas.

	The studio has announced that the U.K. largest Harry Potter shop will open in central London in November, weeks before the hotly-anticipated series premieres on Dec. 25. 

	The flagship store, which will span two floors and more than 21,000 square-feet, will be located on the main shopping area of Oxford Street and has, according to Warner Bros., taken inspiration from the Wizarding World’s own magical shopping street Diagon Alley. It is set to feature a dragon towering above Gringotts bank, a full-sized Knight Bus and also a branch of the Leaky Cauldron pub serving food and foaming Butterbeer.
	

	“There’s no better place to create a destination that celebrates the magic, creativity and storytelling that has captivated generations of fans around the world,” said Karl Durrant, Warner Bros,’ senior vice-president of worldwide retail, in a statement, adding that the opening of the store was “a truly special milestone.”


	The Oxford Street location will become the second official Harry Potter store in the U.K. after the site at King’s Cross Station, where Potter and his fellow young wizards famously catch the train to Hogwarts. But the new store will reportedly include various exclusives, including a Diagon Alley wand, a special Funko Pop and a MinaLima artwork inspired by the Knight Bus and Diagon Alley.

	Alongside the official shops, there are numerous other unofficial stores selling Potter-themed merchandise scattered around London city center and other tourist hotspots. Perhaps coincidentally (or perhaps a sign of a darker wizarding power in the commercial sector), less than a day before the news of the Oxford Street store was announced, one of these unofficial stores was reported to have closed down.

schema.headline: U.K.’s Largest Harry Potter Store Opening in London Ahead of HBO Series Launch

title: Beatrice Gibson Questions Motherhood and Womanhood in Her Debut Feature ‘At Night’
description: “I am a tone of voice, warming, shifting, pausing, changing, including, asserting, exulting, including, turning and including.” This quote by the po
body:
“I am a tone of voice, warming, shifting, pausing, changing, including, asserting, exulting, including, turning and including.” This quote by the poet Alice Notley opens “At Night,” British filmmaker Beatrice Gibson’s feature debut, which held its world premiere on Aug. 8 in Locarno’s Filmmakers of the Present program. 

	Gibson, who was a friend of Notley’s, took inspiration from the poet’s 1992 feminist epic “The Descent of Alette,” as well as Kathy Acker’s “Don Quixote,” to craft her story about a group of women crossing each other’s paths over the course of a single night in Paris.   
	

	Poetry doesn’t just open the film; it shapes the entire narrative. “[Notley] was always talking about non-compliance,” Gibson says, highlighting poetry’s ability to accommodate formal and thematic experimentation. In “At Night,” poetry appears in staged performances, voiceovers, and moments in between, as when we hear an off-screen female voice reciting a poem, then watch a character pause on a dark street corner to watch a video of that reading. In these instances, poetry becomes a sonic bridge connecting disparate characters, spaces, and stories.




	

					‘At Night’
									Courtesy of Night Films Ltd
	



	“At Night” is anchored by the relationship between Bea (played by Gibson), a filmmaker on a location-scouting trip in Paris, and Didi (Diocouda Diaoune), who used to work with and for Bea. Their relationship has strained along racial and class lines; in one pivotal scene, they openly discuss the weight of these structural pressures on their relationship. Their tension allows Gibson to explore the “polarities and asymmetries,” as she calls them, that emerge from the “intersectional gathering of people” driving her project. 
	

	“I come from an art world context, which is kind of a privilege, because you’re taught to stay with the trouble,” Gibson says, about her decision to openly depict the power imbalance between Bea, a successful white artist, and Didi, a Black single mother living in emergency housing. For Gibson, the way to reckon with this disparity was to “make it a part of the film and not run away from it.” The film’s poetic structure broaches such thorny topics without rushing toward easy resolution. “It’s a film in the shape of a question,” Gibson clarifies. “It’s asking how to be inside these crushing polarities.” 

	Gibson describes “At Night” as a “collective autofiction.” Beginning with a voicemail from Bea to Didi, the protagonist’s subjective “I” broadens to encompass a larger cast of women. In one sequence, a group of women from various walks of life sit around a restaurant table discussing their experiences of motherhood and sex. Their discussion resembles the feminist consciousness-raising sessions of the 1970s, which influenced the structure of the film, particularly via Nell Dunn’s 1965 book “Talking to Women.” 

	It mattered to Gibson to depict women facing what would conventionally be termed a “midlife crisis,” but which Gibson prefers to call “midlife revelation.” “It’s a stage [of women’s lives] you don’t see represented that often in cinema, and it’s existentially fantastic,” she says. 

	If the language of poetry serves as the film’s structural base, its grainy analogue footage, shot by Ben Rivers, gives it the texture of a dream. One sequence shows a montage of Paris at night: an illuminated metro entrance, a corner shop with its shutters half-drawn, autumn leaves swirling across empty streets. In the quiet, we hear the whirring of the analogue camera. That sound underscores the physicality of the medium and heightens the sensation of time passing. “Shooting on analogue makes everything present tense,” Gibson says. “It’s not like digital logic, where you expect a distinct outcome. It’s about just being in space with these characters.”

	Gibson’s focus on the particularities of her characters’ experiences is one way in which the feminist maxim “the personal is political” emerges in the film. But the notion also informs Gibson’s approach to depicting motherhood, a theme that occupies the center of the film while simultaneously existing at its margins: No children appear, but we watch as a woman takes a muffled phone call with her daughter or sends a late-night text reminding her partner to pick up baby food. The women in “At Night” experience motherhood in various ways, whether reveling in it, dodging it, or even grieving its loss. 
	

	“[The women] are escaping in this non-compliant, non-conformist way,” Gibson explains. “The characters are constructed to do things they shouldn’t be doing.” Bea’s character, for example, “temporarily [abandons] the nuclear family structure” to work on her film. When motherhood is no longer defined as a duty, new possibilities for female selfhood emerge. Through these distinct lives and their collective weight, “At Night” treats womanhood and motherhood not as fixed destinations, but as living, ongoing questions.

schema.headline: Beatrice Gibson Questions Motherhood and Womanhood in Her Debut Feature ‘At Night’

title: AI Music Generator Suno Strikes Licensing Deal With BMG as It Preps New Label-Backed Models
description: Suno, the AI music generator that’s managed to both rankle the music industry and lure some of its biggest talent to its side, has added music compa
body:
Suno, the AI music generator that’s managed to both rankle the music industry and lure some of its biggest talent to its side, has added music company BMG as its latest licensing partner as it prepares new models powered by licensed work.

	The partnership will see Suno pay for BMG’s repertoire of recordings from its artists, while also covering the use of any BMG songs to train Suno’s past models. BMG joins Warner Music Group in settling with the music-generation company, which has been the target of a series of lawsuits alleging unauthorized use of audio recordings to train its data.
	

	“We believe the future of music will be more participatory, creating entirely new ways for artists and fans to connect,” Suno CEO and co-founder Mikey Shulman said in a statement. “Building that future responsibly means working directly with the people who make music and the companies that represent them. Together with BMG, we can develop new experiences that give artists and songwriters real choice, generate new revenue, and make music a bigger part of people’s lives.”


	Celine Joshua, BMG’s executive vice president of global marketing and streaming, framed music’s future as one where artists and songwriters “share in the value” platforms such as Suno may create.

	“Choice is the guiding principle,” Joshua said. “This agreement establishes strong protections, clear economics, and new creative possibilities for artists and their fans. As we enter the era of creation, we look forward to shaping that future together with our creators and Suno.” 
	

	The settlement marks BMG’s most notable acceptance of AI’s role in music since the generative era began. It sued Anthropic in California federal court earlier this year for allegedly using its copyrighted works, including songs by the likes of Bruno Mars and the Rolling Stones, to train its models in what it called a scheme of “widespread and systematic infringement.” The case, similar to one brought by other music publishers in 2023, is ongoing.

	BMG also joined a collection of other music labels and companies last month, including WMG, Universal Music Group and Sony Music, in proposing a new set of guidelines for how AI-generated music could chart on music tracking lists, specifying that only tracks that were “substantially human made” qualify for the industry’s measure of success.

	The deal with BMG also gives Suno another layer of legitimacy as it prepares its new industry-backed models, which Suno said on Monday would come soon. Last week, Suno said it would begin watermarking songs downloaded from the platform to help signify the use of AI and limit song downloads for its three usage tiers to combat slop, efforts the company is taking to further legitimize its outputs among the music industry.

	Still, Suno is facing ongoing lawsuits from UMG and Sony Music for copyright infringement, and last month a German court found that the company was violating U.S. and German copyright laws.

schema.headline: AI Music Generator Suno Strikes Licensing Deal With BMG as It Preps New Label-Backed Models

title: ‘In Flames’ Director Zarrar Kahn Returns to Toronto With Gym-Incel Rom-Com ‘The Lion Does Not Concern Himself,’ Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Zarrar Kahn, whose debut feature “In Flames” premiered at Cannes and later played Toronto, is returning to the festival’s Short Cuts strand with rom
body:
Zarrar Kahn, whose debut feature “In Flames” premiered at Cannes and later played Toronto, is returning to the festival’s Short Cuts strand with romantic comedy “The Lion Does Not Concern Himself.” 

	A trailer has been unveiled.

	The film follows a likeable gym coach who has convinced himself that his identity as a toxic podcaster is his only route to cultural relevance – until someone walks in as a new client and stays as a love interest. The concept originated with Mohammad Ali Hashmi, the film’s Toronto-based writer and lead actor and a frequent Kahn collaborator, who was struck by the volume of incel propaganda he encountered upon joining a new gym, and by how readily a gym regular could become an Andrew Tate champion.
	

	Kahn found the subject compelling but chose to reframe the familiar terrain of male anger and online isolation as a classic rom-com. The title, drawn from a “Game of Thrones” line that has since gone viral on TikTok, is a tongue-in-cheek reference to manosphere culture – and to that culture’s own capacity to poke fun at itself.


	“The film is sort of about the manosphere, sort of about the gender divide, and sort of about the inherent goofiness of falling in love,” Kahn said in a director’s statement.

	Kahn directed, co-wrote, and co-edited the film, shot at a gym on Queen West in Toronto. 

	Lauren Saarimaki of POV Film produces, with Mina Husain of Suno Studios executive producing. CityLights Media handles world sales and festivals – the same company behind Kahn’s forthcoming climate thriller “Suffering Is Optional,” starring “Ms. Marvel” breakout Iman Vellani, which is set to begin production in early 2027.
	

	Watch the trailer for “The Lion Does Not Concern Himself” here:

schema.headline: ‘In Flames’ Director Zarrar Kahn Returns to Toronto With Gym-Incel Rom-Com ‘The Lion Does Not Concern Himself,’ Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Alex Cooper and Matt Kaplan’s Unwell Media Company Valued at $500 Million After Investment From Patrick Whitesell’s WTSL
description: Unwell, the media company co-founded by married couple Alex Cooper and Matt Kaplan, has landed its first outside investor: Patrick Whitesell, co-fou
body:
Unwell, the media company co-founded by married couple Alex Cooper and Matt Kaplan, has landed its first outside investor: Patrick Whitesell, co-founder of WME and former executive chairman of successor company Endeavor.

	Whitesell’s WTSL, an investment firm focused on media, entertainment and sports he launched after exiting Endeavor and WME last year, has invested an undisclosed sum in Unwell that values the business at $500 million, according to Unwell. Cooper and Kaplan, who self-funded the company targeting Gen Z women audiences, retain a majority ownership stake. Formed in 2023, Unwell says it has been profitable from day one and sees the WTSL investment as growth capital.
	

	Unwell said that in addition to the funding, WTSL brings “deep strategic expertise, industry relationships and a proven track record of supporting some of the most innovative companies and storytellers in media,” including Peyton Manning’s Omaha Productions.


	“Trust has become the ultimate distribution channel and 70 million women a month tune into Unwell,” Cooper, whose “Call Her Daddy” podcast remains the company’s tentpole franchise. “We’re scaling on all fronts, combining nimbleness, social-first premium content, and our understanding of culture to serve this highly influential audience. With WTSL’s backing, the company is now also poised to accelerate our media platform’s growth through acquisitions and investments.”

	Whitesell said in a statement, “Alex, Matt and the team have demonstrated an exceptional ability to anticipate where audiences are headed and create entertainment experiences that resonate deeply,” he said. “The company’s growth, audience connection and cultural relevance set it apart, and we believe Unwell is uniquely positioned to help define the present and future of media.”
	



	

					Alex Cooper and Patrick Whitesell
									Photo credit: Michela Pini/Unwell
	



	News of the funding from Whitesell’s WTSL comes after a pair of recent exposés alleging behind-the-scenes chaos at Unwell. According to a Vanity Fair story in June, one Unwell freelancer alleged that Kaplan “creates the most toxic work environment that I’ve ever seen”; anonymous sources also said Kaplan had questioned employees about their sex lives and commented on their physical appearance. In April, Bloomberg reported that Kaplan “has earned a reputation for frequently yelling at staff members” and said Unwell’s employees were “looking for the exit.”

	Cooper, in an interview at Cannes Lions this June with the Wall Street Journal, was asked about the allegations. “I will just kind of leave it at ‘Don’t believe everything that you read on the internet’ — but I think everyone knows that at this point,” she said. Cooper also said, “I think that we have done a really incredible job at Unwell, and I think if you walk the halls, there are so many people that are so happy to work at this company. … I think, unfortunately, being a woman in this industry is extremely difficult because you’re held to a completely different standard. Whether it’s a smear campaign being created for someone’s narrative, whatever it be.”

	Kaplan is the founder of ACE Entertainment, whose credits include “To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before,” one of Netflix’s most-watched original films to date, and popular Gen Z series “XO, Kitty” (also for Netflix).

	“As the premier media company for women, we’re collaborating with some of the biggest brands in the world on creator-led strategies,” Kaplan said in a statement. “Brands realize buying paid ads or influence just isn’t enough in such a disparate media landscape. And, it’s difficult to find a platform like Unwell that meets Gen Z where they are on their terms. That’s something legacy media still hasn’t unlocked.”

	Unwell says its audience is 89% female, with 72% between the ages of 18 and 35. The company claims to have nearly 100 million followers across platforms and generated more than 1.7 trillion earned media impressions in 2025 alone. Its podcast network of more than a dozen shows is supported by a “significant” SiriusXM partnership and video engagement on YouTube. In 2024, Cooper inked a three-year deal with SiriusXM worth as much as $125 million over the course of the agreement.
	

	Beyond podcasting, Unwell has expanded into series for premium streaming services and YouTube as well as live events.

	The company produced the “Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special” on Disney +; partnered with Peacock on live programming from the Paris Olympics; launched reality series “Love Overboard” with Hulu, and has a slate of shows with Netflix, including “Let’s Marry Harry” and “Icebreaker,” set to shoot this fall. Unwell also has a growing portfolio of YouTube-native series announced earlier this year at the streaming giant’s Brandcast event.

	Unwell also has staged nationwide tours, spring break experiences, SXSW activations and other live events (which the company estimates have been attended by more than 150,000 fans in person). The company also has a consumer products business spanning energy drinks, hydration products and stick packs.

title: John Gotti's Grandson Gets Prison Time Shaved Off Amid His Mom's Major Health Issues
description:
John Gotti's Grandson
                          Catches A Little Break On Prison Time ...
body:
John Gotti's Grandson
                          Catches A Little Break On Prison Time ...
                          As Clock Ticks On Mom's Kidney Donor Search
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 12, 2026
                            3:50 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 12, 2026
                                5:31 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            John Gotti's grandson Carmine Agnello will have to spend just over a year behind bars as his mom, Victoria Gotti, desperately tries to find a kidney donor during his incarceration, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The federal Bureau of Prisons says Carmine's release date has been pushed up to September 2, 2027, which is a nearly 13-month stretch instead of his original 15-month sentence.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported, Carmine pleaded guilty to a $1.1 wire fraud scheme tied to COVID-19 relief funds in 2024. Carmine surrendered Monday to the feds and was imprisoned at the Federal Correctional Institution Fairton in Fairton, New Jersey.    
      

            Even though he got some time shaved off, Carmine still faces a major hurdle in trying to supply Victoria with his kidney as her health problems mount while he's in prison.
      
    
            As we told you, Carmine was initially supposed to report to prison on July 20, but the judge gave him an extension so he could donate one of his kidneys to his mom. But Victoria got an infection, and the surgery was shelved.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The judge then gave Carmine until August 10 to donate his kidney and report to prison on September 18. But that didn't work either because Victoria couldn't get medically cleared for the procedure.
      
    
            On Monday, Carmine's attorney, Robert Beltrani, filed court documents asking for a third extension, but the judge turned down the request while postponing Carmine's report time to prison by 2 hours.  
      
    
            Our Gotti sources have told us Carmine only wanted to help Victoria by doing the surgery before going to prison as she battles severe complications from kidney disease. We're also told Carmine was not trying to get out of doing his time behind bars.

title: John Hinckley Jr. Sends Jodie Foster Message Decades After Reagan Assassination Attempt
description:
John Hinckley Jr. to Jodie Foster
                          Hope You've Been Well!!!
body:
John Hinckley Jr. to Jodie Foster
                          Hope You've Been Well!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 11, 2026
                            6:12 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            John Hinckley Jr. is still sending Jodie Foster his love ... 45 years after he attempted to assassinate Ronald Reagan to impress her.
      
    
            According to a preview for an upcoming interview on "The Mark Joseph Show" -- obtained by Entertainment Weekly -- Hinckley Jr. says ... "I just wish Jodie Foster well, you know."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He continued ... "I don’t really see her movies, but I wish her well, and I know she’s doing quite well. And that’s all I can say is just, I wish Jodie well, and I hope she has a good life."
      

            Hinckley Jr. shot Reagan in 1981 outside the Hilton Hotel in Washington, D.C., just after the then-president had given a speech.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He claimed at the time that he was trying to impress Jodie with the assassination attempt, allegedly inspired by her movie "Taxi Driver."
      
    
            In the movie, the actress played a child prostitute alongside Robert De Niro, whose character attempted to assassinate a presidential candidate.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hinckley was ultimately found not guilty by reason of insanity and spent decades in a psychiatric facility at St. Elizabeths Hospital.
      
    
            He was released with conditions in 2016, and in 2022 a federal judge approved his release without conditions.

Goth Girl From Drake Dating Show
                          He's Really Buying My Mom a House!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 12, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Drake is putting his money where his mouth is ... the "goth baddie" who won his speed dating challenge says he's making good on his promise to buy her mother a new home.
      
    
            The apple of Champagne Papi's eye -- content creator and OnlyFans model Pinkchyu -- tells TMZ ... Drake is going to make good on his word and all she has to do is pick out a listing and he'll take care of the payment.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            While Pinkchyu won Drizzy's "20-v-1" dating show and made him bark like a dog ... she says they didn't end up up hooking up ... even after all the flirting and role playing.
      

            Pinkchyu was pretty coy about whether or not she had plans of seeing Drake again, but said they had some good conversations at the after party and it's safe to say something is in the works.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Drake is clearly super into Pinkchyu, but she tells us she isn't necessarily a big fan of his music ... and knew him mainly from his 'Degrassi' days.
      
    
            No word on timing for a big real estate purchase, but she says she's making a lot more money thanks to Drake ... telling us her OF subscriptions are through the roof after going viral.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            Pinkchyu isn't sure how she's even made it to this point ... although she admits getting hotter hasn't hurt ... and she has even bigger dreams of getting into the music industry.
